forces.title: Decelerating GDP growth reduces demand across key steel end-use sectors
forces.description: India's GDP Annual Growth Rate is at 7.8% but shows a falling trend (-0.2% change over prior period), indicating a deceleration in overall economic activity. This directly impacts the Steel & Ferrous Metals sector by reducing demand across critical end-use sectors such as construction, automotive, and manufacturing, leading to lower consumption and sales volumes. The active and acute negative effect is already biting.

forces.title: Rising 10-Year G-Sec Yield increases borrowing costs for steel projects
forces.description: The 10-Year G-Sec Yield (FBIL) is at 7.08 and rising, having increased by 0.31 over the last three periods. As the steel sector carries India's largest industrial debt and is highly capital-intensive, this rise significantly increases the cost of long-term borrowing for new capacity expansion and refinancing existing debt. This directly raises financing costs, potentially impacting investment decisions and overall profitability for steelmakers. The effect is just starting to bite with acute intensity.
forces.source_title: Building India’s next 100 MTPA - Embedding execution excellence in steel projects

forces.title: Robust fixed investment boosts demand for steel in infrastructure and construction
forces.description: Gross Fixed Capital Formation (GFCF) Annual at Current Prices is rising, currently at 27902.73 INR Billion and up 3691.5 INR Billion over three periods. This indicates robust economy-wide fixed investment, directly boosting demand for steel in construction, infrastructure, and capital goods manufacturing. This translates into increased steel consumption, with reports of an 8% year-on-year increase for construction and infrastructure. This active, acute positive effect is already biting.

forces.title: BF-BOF route remains dominant due to green steel viability challenges
forces.description: Globally, BF-BOF technology accounts for 70% of crude steel production, and 90% in China. Despite environmental concerns, BF-BOF is increasingly adopted in India due to abundant low-cost coal and strong domestic demand, and limited natural gas/scrap availability. JSW Steel notes that green steel is not yet economically viable at scale in India due to high renewable power costs and limited energy storage, making BF-BOF the most scalable and reliable option for large-capacity creation in the near-to-medium term. This is a foundational structural element of India's steel production.
forces.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

forces.title: Ferrous scrap becoming strategic resource for cost stability and decarbonization
forces.description: Ferrous scrap is no longer a secondary material but a strategic raw material for Indian steelmakers. It directly reduces dependence on carbon-intensive raw materials (iron ore, coking coal, fossil fuels), lowering emissions on a commercial scale without waiting for technological breakthroughs. From a cost standpoint, it reduces exposure to raw material and logistics volatility. India's scrap consumption is 41 MMT, but only contributes 23% to steel manufacturing (vs. 32% global average), indicating significant room for increased adoption to improve resource security and sustainability.
forces.source_title: Why ferrous scrap is becoming a strategic lever for Indian steelmakers

forces.title: Energy costs significantly impact DRI-EAF steel production competitiveness
forces.description: Energy costs (natural gas and electricity) are the primary determinant of competitiveness for DRI-EAF steel production. For one ton of hot-rolled coil, about 11 gigajoules of natural gas and 700 kilowatt hours of electricity are required. Locations with high gas prices, like Sweden (four to five times higher than Oman) and Germany (two to three times higher than Oman), face substantial cost disadvantages. India’s gas prices are roughly double Oman's, adding 10-20% to steel prices, which constrains the adoption of this lower-emission technology.
forces.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

forces.title: Government capital expenditure boosts demand for steel products
forces.description: Increased government capital expenditure directly fuels infrastructure and construction projects, leading to higher demand for steel products. India's growth trajectory, anchored in strong domestic demand and supported by structural reforms, benefits significantly from government spending on highways, railways, and industrial corridors. This sustained public investment is a key demand driver, providing a stable and growing market for the Steel & Ferrous Metals sector's output, ensuring sustained growth momentum and utilization of expanded capacity.

forces.title: PLI Scheme and green steel initiatives bolster sector growth
forces.description: The Production Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme, particularly PLI 1.2 for specialty steel, has attracted significant investments (Rs. 23,022 crore) and aims to create 8.7 million tonnes of additional specialty steel capacity by FY31. This initiative, alongside growing green steel demand (forecasted to reach 4.49 MT by FY30), strengthens domestic production, reduces import dependence, and enhances global competitiveness. These policy-driven incentives act as a strong tailwind, supporting high-end segments and long-term sustainable growth for the Indian steel sector.

forces.title: Project execution delays and cost overruns hinder capacity expansion targets
forces.description: India's ambitious target of 300 MTPA crude steel capacity by 2030 is challenged by persistent project execution issues. Many recent steel projects have experienced schedule delays (15-80% time variance), cost escalations, and execution bottlenecks. These stem from fragmented strategies, delayed engineering readiness, weak design-procurement alignment, over-reliance on in-situ construction, and limited digital interventions. The shortage of skilled manpower further impacts productivity, creating a significant headwind that risks diluting the effectiveness of substantial capital investments.
forces.source_title: Building India’s next 100 MTPA - Embedding execution excellence in steel projects

forces.title: AI adoption enhancing mining safety and productivity for steel inputs
forces.description: The mining industry, which supplies critical inputs like iron ore and coking coal for steel, is increasingly adopting AI tools for safety transformation. Automation, remote monitoring, and agentic AI systems are improving hazard identification, worker behavior, and contractor management. These technologies, ranging from autonomous drones mapping shafts to AI-enabled video analytics and digital twins, reduce human exposure to risks, enhance operational discipline, and increase productivity. This structural shift, though broader than steel, improves the reliability and efficiency of raw material supply for steelmakers, enhancing long-term operational performance and safety.
forces.source_title: Harnessing AI to make mining safer

forces.title: INR depreciation increases import costs for raw materials
forces.description: The USD/INR exchange rate at 95.23405, with a 0.956% change over the prior period, is increasing the cost of imported raw materials like coking coal, iron ore, and other fossil fuels. India is highly dependent on imports for coking coal, which is a primary input for blast furnace steel production. This directly raises production costs for steelmakers, compressing margins and impacting overall profitability. This active and moderately intense negative effect is already biting.

forces.title: Global overcapacity in steel production compresses margins
forces.description: In 2024, the global steel industry had the capacity to produce over 2.5 billion tons, while demand was only about 1.9 billion tons. Much of this excess capacity, primarily in China, has historically compressed margins for steel producers worldwide. This persistent overcapacity creates a challenging market environment, limiting pricing power and profitability for Indian steelmakers, even amid strong domestic demand. This fundamental imbalance acts as a headwind, forcing companies to focus intensely on cost efficiency and competitive positioning.
forces.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

forces.title: Infrastructure, automotive, and renewables drive robust materials demand
forces.description: After a period of flat demand, steel, aluminum, copper, and stainless steel are expected to return to sustained growth by 2030, driven by several structural forces. Geopolitical realignment is leading to reshoring, increasing domestic materials demand. Decarbonization redefines material specifications, boosting demand for 'green metals'. New technologies like AI-driven data centers, EVs, and renewable energy infrastructure generate sustained high demand for quality materials, requiring higher capabilities from service centers. This broad demand surge creates a tailwind for the steel sector.
forces.source_title: The next wave of value in the materials supply chain

forces.title: Technological innovations enhance efficiency and sustainability in steel production
forces.description: The Indian steel industry is increasingly emphasizing technological innovations to improve efficiency, sustainability, and safety across the value chain. Initiatives include inviting AI startups for technology-driven solutions, trial injection of hydrogen gas in blast furnaces (Tata Steel), adoption of alternative hot metal production technologies (Hismelt, Finex, ITmk3), and R&D projects with at least 1% of sales turnover. Energy efficiency improvement projects for obsolete mills are also underway. These advancements are a tailwind, enhancing operational performance, reducing environmental impact, and bolstering India's position in global steel production.

forces.title: Shift towards industrialized project delivery key for capacity expansion
forces.description: India's steel sector must transition from conventional, labor-intensive construction models to modular and industrialized execution methodologies to meet its 300 MTPA capacity target efficiently. This involves greater adoption of modularization, standardized designs, offsite fabrication, and value engineering, combined with early design freeze. Such practices, exemplified by China's success in reducing project timelines by 20-30%, will lower manpower intensity, improve safety, compress schedules, and enhance overall project predictability and capital efficiency, representing a crucial structural shift for India's growth ambitions.
forces.source_title: Building India’s next 100 MTPA - Embedding execution excellence in steel projects

forces.title: Fragmented scrap ecosystem limits quality, scale, and traceability
forces.description: India's ferrous scrap ecosystem is fragmented and informal, which significantly limits the quality, scale, and traceability of scrap. This impacts effective scrap utilization, preventing the steel industry from fully capitalizing on scrap as a strategic resource for decarbonization and cost stability. This structural weakness acts as a headwind, increasing reliance on more carbon-intensive raw materials and hindering the development of a resilient, circular, and low-carbon domestic steel industry. Formalization and technology are needed to unlock its full potential.
forces.source_title: Why ferrous scrap is becoming a strategic lever for Indian steelmakers

viewpoints.title: India's steel growth hinges on execution excellence, not just investment commitments
viewpoints.description: India's steel sector is poised for significant growth, targeting 300 MTPA by 2030, a crucial phase for industrial development. However, achieving this goal requires a critical shift from investment commitments to actual project execution. Past projects have faced delays and cost escalations, highlighting the need for robust planning, governance, and efficient delivery. The industry must rethink how projects are planned and executed, emphasizing standardisation, modular construction, and digital tools to ensure timely and budget-bound capacity creation.
viewpoints.source_title: Building India’s next 100 MTPA: Embedding execution excellence in steel project delivery

viewpoints.title: Government foresees significant growth potential for India's steel sector through policy support
viewpoints.description: The Indian government highlighted significant growth opportunities for the steel sector, targeting 500 MT production capacity by 2047. This ambition is underpinned by rising domestic demand from infrastructure, construction, and automotive sectors, expanding exports, and strong policy support through PLI incentives. Additionally, green steel initiatives and greater global market access are expected to bolster the sector, indicating a positive long-term outlook for robust domestic production and self-reliance in specialty steel.

viewpoints.title: Stainless steel crucial for India's infrastructure, mobility, and defence growth
viewpoints.description: India's steel industry is entering a defining phase of growth, with capacity targeting 300 MTPA by 2030. Within this, stainless steel is seen as increasingly important for infrastructure, mobility, energy, industrial, and defence applications. As India aims to become a global manufacturing hub and self-reliant, the demand for high-quality, corrosion-resistant, reliable, and sustainable materials will grow. This necessitates strengthening domestic stainless steel capabilities and fostering its ecosystem through investment, innovation, and category awareness.
viewpoints.source_title: Building India’s next 100 MTPA - Embedding execution excellence in steel projects

viewpoints.title: India's steel future depends on execution discipline for capacity expansion
viewpoints.description: India's steel sector is in a defining decade, with the journey from 200 to 300 MTPA testing its collective ability to deliver with precision, speed, and discipline. While investment momentum is strong, translating these investments into timely, cost-efficient, and high-quality operational assets is paramount. Institutionalizing robust execution frameworks, strengthening engineering readiness, adopting integrated delivery models, and enhancing governance are essential. Building capabilities across contractors, engineering partners, and the workforce will determine predictable results at scale.
viewpoints.source_title: Building India’s next 100 MTPA - Embedding execution excellence in steel projects

viewpoints.title: Capacity commissioning and asset performance are true tests of industrial capability
viewpoints.description: India's steel sector's success is measured by its ability to translate investment ambition into outcomes: capacity commissioned on time, assets performing as designed, and projects generating lasting economic and social value. As projects grow in scale and complexity, meticulous planning and execution discipline become critical. Front-end engineering, early layout validation, clear execution philosophies, and robust institutional systems are essential to reduce rework, align stakeholders, and ensure predictable delivery. The strength of India's steel sector hinges on effective implementation by all stakeholders.
viewpoints.source_title: Building India’s next 100 MTPA - Embedding execution excellence in steel projects

viewpoints.title: BF-BOF remains essential for large-scale capacity amid green steel challenges
viewpoints.description: India's steel industry is at a defining moment, aiming for 300 MTPA capacity by 2030. JSW Steel recognizes the necessity of this expansion for nation-building but highlights structural challenges. Green steel is not yet economically viable at scale in India due to high costs and limited renewable energy. Therefore, the blast furnace–basic oxygen furnace (BF–BOF) route remains the only scalable and reliable option for large-capacity creation in the near to medium term, despite ongoing efforts to improve its sustainability.
viewpoints.source_title: Building India’s next 100 MTPA - Embedding execution excellence in steel projects

viewpoints.title: Ferrous scrap is a strategic lever for Indian steelmakers' decarbonization and cost goals
viewpoints.description: Ferrous scrap has evolved from a secondary material to a strategic resource for Indian steelmakers, addressing decarbonization, cost stability, and supply resilience. Higher scrap adoption reduces dependence on carbon-intensive raw materials like iron ore and coking coal, immediately cutting emissions without major capital investment. Despite India's fragmented scrap ecosystem, formalization and technology can improve quality, traceability, and green steel credibility. Policy, procurement reform, and partnerships are essential to build a resilient, circular, and low-carbon domestic steel industry.
viewpoints.source_title: Why ferrous scrap is becoming a strategic lever for Indian steelmakers
